Multistatic ISAC with Deep Learning-Based Clutter Suppression for 5G and Beyond

Yalin E. Sagduyu Affiliation: Nexcepta, Gaithersburg, MD, USA    Tugba Erpek Affiliation: Nexcepta, Gaithersburg, MD, USA Affiliation: Nexcepta, Gaithersburg, MD, USA    Sastry Kompella Affiliation: Nexcepta, Gaithersburg, MD, USA
Abstract

Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems using 5G and beyond signals of opportunity enable joint wireless sensing and communication using shared infrastructure and spectrum resources. While multistatic ISAC can increase sensing coverage with spatially distributed receivers, dense and dynamic clutter can significantly degrade bistatic range and Doppler estimation, leading to errors in target localization and velocity estimation. This paper presents a multistatic ISAC framework with clutter suppression for high-fidelity estimation of target position and velocity. Distributed clutter is modeled with randomly located scatterers with varying Doppler spreads and radar cross sections to capture dense and dynamic clutter effects. A broad range of conventional signal processing baselines are evaluated for clutter suppression, showing limited robustness under strong clutter conditions. To address this limitation, deep learning-based clutter suppression methods are introduced to improve robustness against dense and dynamic clutter by employing residual and attention-enhanced deep neural network architectures that directly enhance target responses from clutter-contaminated observations. These methods substantially outperform conventional approaches in target position and velocity estimation across diverse clutter conditions in multistatic ISAC.

Index Terms: 
ISAC, multistatic, deep learning, 5G, 6G, localization, velocity estimation, clutter suppression.

I Introduction

Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) is a key technology for next-generation wireless networks that repurposes communication signals for sensing using shared spectrum and infrastructure [1]. An important advantage of ISAC is the ability to exploit signals of opportunity, such as commercial 5G NR signals, for target sensing and detection [2, 3, 4]. In particular, 5G NR positioning reference signals (PRS) provide structured pilot patterns that can be effectively repurposed for passive sensing without dedicated radar transmitters and support persistent low-cost sensing over large areas [5]. The ISAC capabilities are particularly important for mission-critical applications such as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), border monitoring, and counter-unmanned aerial systems (counter-UAS), which require robust sensing, localization, and tracking in complex environments.

Monostatic ISAC systems employ co-located transmitters and receivers, which simplifies synchronization and signal processing but limits sensing coverage and geometric diversity [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. In contrast, multistatic ISAC systems use spatially distributed receivers observing reflections from a common transmitter, enabling improved spatial diversity, wider coverage, enhanced target observability, and more accurate localization [11, 12]. Despite these advantages, multistatic ISAC sensing remains challenging in dense clutter environments, where delayed and Doppler-shifted clutter reflections can overlap with target returns in bistatic range-Doppler space. Since clutter characteristics can vary across spatially distributed receivers, clutter can significantly degrade target localization and velocity estimation performance [13, 14].

In this paper, we study multistatic ISAC with 5G NR PRS in clutter environments for bistatic range-Doppler estimation, two-dimensional (2D) target localization, and velocity estimation using spatially distributed receivers. A multistatic sensing framework based on cross-ambiguity-function (CAF) processing and nonlinear multilateration is adopted. The clutter is introduced using distributed scatterers with randomized locations, radar cross sections (RCSs), and Doppler spreads to capture diverse clutter conditions including highly dynamic clutter with significant Doppler overlap with target returns. We show that conventional signal processing-based clutter suppression methods can only provide partial improvement and their effectiveness drops under dense or dynamic clutter conditions that degrade multistatic ISAC performance.

To improve robustness, we introduce deep learning (DL)-based clutter suppression methods to directly enhance target responses from clutter-contaminated observations. The first method employs a residual U-Net architecture for target-enhanced residual estimation, while the second method introduces directional convolutional processing and attention-gated feature fusion to further improve clutter suppression, target enhancement, and multistatic sensing performance. We show that the proposed residual and attention-aware DL methods substantially outperform conventional clutter suppression approaches across a wide range of clutter conditions, achieving significantly improved bistatic range-Doppler estimation, target localization, and velocity estimation performance.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II presents signal and clutter models. Sec. III describes position and velocity estimation. Sec. IV discusses conventional clutter suppression. Sec. V presents DL-based clutter suppression. Section V evaluates performance. Sec. VII concludes the paper.

II Multistatic ISAC Signal and Clutter Model

We consider an illuminator (base station) that transmits 5G NR PRS and M=3M\!=\!3 distributed receivers that cooperatively process the reflected signals for 2D sensing, as shown in Fig. 1. 5G numerology 0 is assumed as in [11] with subcarrier spacing Δ​f=15​kHz\Delta f\!=\!15~\mathrm{kHz}, FFT size N=1024N\!=\!1024, carrier frequency fc=2.5​GHzf_{c}\!=\!2.5~\mathrm{GHz}, and sampling rate fs=15.36​MHzf_{s}\!=\!15.36~\mathrm{MHz}. The PRS spans KRB=76K_{\mathrm{RB}}\!=\!76 resource blocks and follows the 3GPP TS 38.211 generation procedure using QPSK Gold sequences [15]. Resource allocation uses a comb structure with spacing Kcomb=2K_{\mathrm{comb}}\!\!=\!\!2 and offset koffset=0k_{\mathrm{offset}}\!=\!0, excluding the DC subcarrier. Each NR slot contains 14 OFDM symbols, including LPRS=2L_{\mathrm{PRS}}\!=\!2 PRS symbols. Consecutive PRS transmissions across multiple slots produce K=128K\!\!=\!\!128 coherent slow-time sensing observations.

For receiver m∈{1,2,3}m\in\{1,2,3\}, the bistatic propagation length is

Bm​(𝐩)=‖𝐩−𝐭‖+‖𝐩−𝐫m‖,B_{m}(\mathbf{p})=\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{t}\|+\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{r}_{m}\|, (1)

where 𝐭\mathbf{t} is the transmitter location, 𝐫m\mathbf{r}_{m} is the receiver mm position, 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} are target position and velocity (all in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}).

The associated bistatic radial velocity at receiver mm is

vm​(𝐩,𝐯)=𝐯⊤​(𝐩−𝐭‖𝐩−𝐭‖+𝐩−𝐫m‖𝐩−𝐫m‖),v_{m}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v}^{\top}\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{t}}{\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{t}\|}+\frac{\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{r}_{m}}{\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{r}_{m}\|}\right), (2)

where (⋅)⊤(\cdot)^{\top} denotes transpose. This represents the projection of the target velocity vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} onto the bistatic observation direction associated with receiver mm. The resulting Doppler shift at receiver mm is

fd,m=fcc​vm​(𝐩,𝐯),f_{d,m}=\frac{f_{c}}{c}v_{m}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{v}), (3)

where cc is the speed of light. The sensing region contains NcN_{c} randomly distributed clutter scatterers. The qq-th clutter scatterer with RCS σq(c)\sigma_{q}^{(c)} is located at 𝐜q∈ℝ2\mathbf{c}_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. The clutter RCS values are modeled as independent log-uniform random variables whose scale is controlled by the clutter-strength parameter αc\alpha_{c}, with larger αc\alpha_{c} corresponding to stronger clutter returns. Each scatterer contributes a receiver-dependent Doppler component

fm,q(c)∼𝒩⁡(0,σf,c2),f_{m,q}^{(c)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{f,c}^{2}), (4)

where fm,q(c)f_{m,q}^{(c)} is a zero-mean Gaussian random variable with variance σf,c2\sigma_{f,c}^{2} and σf,c\sigma_{f,c} controls the clutter Doppler spread. Larger σf,c\sigma_{f,c} yields more dynamic clutter, while larger NcN_{c} yields denser clutter. The received signal at receiver mm is the superposition of the target echo, clutter reflections, and noise:

ym​[n]\displaystyle y_{m}[n] =αm​s​[n−τm]​ej​2​π​fd,m​n​Ts\displaystyle=\alpha_{m}s[n-\tau_{m}]e^{j2\pi f_{d,m}nT_{s}}
+∑q=1Ncβm,qs[n−τm,q(c)]ej​2​π​fm,q(c)​n​Ts+wm[n],\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{q=1}^{N_{c}}\beta_{m,q}s[n-\tau_{m,q}^{(c)}]e^{j2\pi f_{m,q}^{(c)}nT_{s}}+w_{m}[n], (5)

where s⁡[n]s[n] denotes the transmitted PRS waveform, Ts=1/fsT_{s}=1/f_{s} is the sampling interval, τm\tau_{m} and τm,q(c)\tau_{m,q}^{(c)} denote the target and clutter propagation delays, respectively, αm\alpha_{m} and βm,q\beta_{m,q} are their reflection coefficients, and wm​[n]∼𝒞​𝒩​(0,σn2)w_{m}[n]\!\sim\!\mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma_{n}^{2}) is additive white Gaussian noise. The reflection coefficients account for bistatic propagation loss, antenna gains, carrier wavelength, and target and clutter RCS. With a narrowband approximation, the echo amplitude for a scatterer at location 𝐱\mathbf{x} is modeled as

γ⁡(𝐱)=PT​GT​GR​λ​σ(4​π)3/2​Rtx​Rrx,\gamma(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\sqrt{P_{T}G_{T}G_{R}}\lambda\sqrt{\sigma}}{(4\pi)^{3/2}R_{\mathrm{tx}}R_{\mathrm{rx}}}, (6)

where PTP_{T} is transmit power, GTG_{T} and GRG_{R} are transmit and receive antenna gains, λ=c/fc\lambda\!=\!c/f_{c} is the carrier wavelength, RtxR_{\mathrm{tx}} and RrxR_{\mathrm{rx}} are the transmitter-to-scatterer and scatterer-to-receiver distances, and σ\sigma is the RCS. Before CAF processing, the direct path is estimated and removed from the received signal.

III Target Localization and Velocity Estimation

Each sensing receiver correlates the received samples with the known PRS reference sequence. Let 0≤k≤K−10\leq k\leq K-1 denote the slow-time PRS observation index, tkt_{k} denote the midpoint time of the kk-th PRS symbol, and sk​[n]s_{k}[n], 0≤n≤N−10\leq n\leq N-1, denote the associated cyclic-prefix (CP)-free PRS reference symbol. For delay bin 0≤d≤D−10\leq d\leq D-1, the correlation output is

Cm​(k,d)=∑n=0N−1ym​[nkcp+d+n]​sk∗​[n]C_{m}(k,d)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}y_{m}[n_{k}^{\mathrm{cp}}+d+n]s_{k}^{*}[n] (7)

at receiver mm, where nkcpn_{k}^{\mathrm{cp}} is the starting sample index of the CP-free PRS region for observation kk and (⋅)∗(\cdot)^{*} is the complex conjugate. The resulting matrix 𝐂m∈ℂK×D\mathbf{C}_{m}\!\in\!\mathbb{C}^{K\times D} represents the slow-time delay-response for clutter mitigation and Doppler analysis. Following clutter suppression (see Secs. IV-V), coherent integration is applied over the slow-time dimension using a Doppler grid with Nf=401N_{f}\!=\!401 frequency bins over [−400,400][-400,400] Hz. Using a Hann window W⁡[k]W[k], the CAF is

CAFm​(d,f)=∑k=0K−1W⁡[k]​Cm​(k,d)​e−j​2​π​f​tk\mathrm{CAF}_{m}(d,f)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}W[k]C_{m}(k,d)e^{-j2\pi ft_{k}} (8)

for receiver mm at Doppler frequency ff. The magnitude response |CAFm​(d,f)||\mathrm{CAF}_{m}(d,f)| produces the bistatic range-Doppler map. Target detection uses two-dimensional cell-averaging constant false alarm rate (CA-CFAR) on the CAF magnitude response. Three-point parabolic interpolation around the detected cell is applied in delay and Doppler dimensions to refine bistatic range and radial velocity estimates B^m\hat{B}_{m} and v^m\hat{v}_{m}. Target localization jointly fits the bistatic range measurements from all receivers. Each bistatic measurement defines an ellipse with foci located at the transmitter and the corresponding receiver position. When

ϵm​(𝐩)=‖𝐩−𝐭‖+‖𝐩−𝐫m‖−B^m\epsilon_{m}(\mathbf{p})=\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{t}\|+\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{r}_{m}\|-\hat{B}_{m} (9)

is the bistatic residual associated with receiver mm, the estimated target position is determined from solving

𝐩^=arg⁡min⁡∑m=1M𝐩⁡(ϵm​(𝐩))2.\hat{\mathbf{p}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{p}}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(\epsilon_{m}(\mathbf{p})\right)^{2}. (10)

Because the bistatic constraints are nonlinear, a trust-region reflective least-squares solver with multiple randomized initialization points is employed. The solution yielding the minimum aggregate residual error is selected as the final estimate.

After estimating target position, the bistatic radial velocity relations become linear in the Cartesian velocity vector. Define

𝐮m=𝐩^−𝐭‖𝐩^−𝐭‖+𝐩^−𝐫m‖𝐩^−𝐫m‖,\mathbf{u}_{m}=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{t}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{t}\|}+\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{r}_{m}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{r}_{m}\|}, (11)

as the bistatic observation direction for receiver mm. Stacking these vectors forms the observation matrix 𝐔∈ℝM×2\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times 2}, while the estimated radial velocities are collected into

𝐯^r=[v^1,…,v^M]⊤.\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{r}}=[\hat{v}_{1},\ldots,\hat{v}_{M}]^{\top}. (12)

The Cartesian velocity is estimated using ridge-regularized least squares (with a small regularization parameter ε>0\varepsilon\!>\!0)

𝐯^=(𝐔⊤​𝐔+ε​𝐈)−1​𝐔⊤​𝐯^r,\hat{\mathbf{v}}=\left(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U}+\varepsilon\mathbf{I}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{r}}, (13)

where 𝐈\mathbf{I} is the identity matrix. The target speed is given by ‖𝐯^‖\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}\| and the heading angle is computed using atan2⁡(v^y,v^x)\operatorname{atan2}(\hat{v}_{y},\hat{v}_{x}).

IV Baselines for Clutter Suppression

We next compare a broad set of conventional clutter suppression methods operating on the slow-time delay correlation matrix 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m}. They suppress clutter using techniques like temporal differencing, subspace projection, Doppler-domain filtering, adaptive prediction, and smooth-component estimation. After clutter suppression, the resulting correlation matrices are used for CAF computation and bistatic range-Doppler estimation.

IV-1 No Clutter Suppression (NCS)

NCS skips clutter mitigation and computes the CAF from the correlation matrix 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m}.

IV-2 Current-Reference Subtraction (CUR)

CUR serves as a coherent reference-based clutter suppression benchmark. Let 𝐂mcur\mathbf{C}_{m}^{\mathrm{cur}} denote the current clutter-contaminated correlation matrix and 𝐂mref\mathbf{C}_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}} denote the clutter-only reference correlation matrix for receiver mm. A global clutter phase offset ϕm\phi_{m} is estimated from dominant clutter components in the reference and current observations. The current observation is phase-aligned prior to subtraction, yielding the clutter-suppressed correlation matrix

𝐂mCUR=e−j​ϕm​𝐂mcur−𝐂mref.\mathbf{C}_{m}^{\mathrm{CUR}}=e^{-j\phi_{m}}\mathbf{C}_{m}^{\mathrm{cur}}-\mathbf{C}_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}}. (14)

The clutter-suppressed matrix 𝐂mCUR\mathbf{C}_{m}^{\mathrm{CUR}} is used for CAF computation according to (8) to estimate bistatic range and Doppler.

IV-3 Space-Projection Adaptive Difference (SP-AD)

SP-AD suppresses slowly varying clutter by differencing adjacent slow-time snapshots prior to CAF processing.

IV-4 Rank-One Slow-Time Projection (SP-R1)

SP-R1 models clutter as a dominant rank-one slow-time component and removes the strongest singular mode before Doppler processing.

IV-5 DPSS Band-Stop Filtering (DPSS)

Discrete prolate spheroidal sequences (DPSS) model clutter as a low-Doppler process and aim to suppress clutter by projecting the signal onto the orthogonal complement of a DPSS clutter subspace.

IV-6 Clutter Map Temporal Doppler Filtering (CMTD)

CMTD suppresses near-zero-Doppler clutter using FFT-based slow-time notch filtering centered near zero frequency.

IV-7 Total Variation High-Pass Filtering (TVHP)

TVHP models clutter as a temporally smooth component and removes smooth clutter responses using total-variation regularization.

IV-8 Rolling-Median High-Pass Filtering (RMHP)

RMHP suppresses clutter using a sliding-window median filter along the slow-time dimension to remove slowly varying clutter responses while preserving localized target peaks.

IV-9 Wavelet High-Pass Filtering (WHP)

WHP applies Haar wavelet decomposition along slow time and reconstructs the signal using high-frequency detail components.

IV-10 Adaptive Least Mean Squares (LMS) Residual Filtering (ALMS)

ALMS applies adaptive LMS prediction along slow time and uses the prediction residual for clutter suppression.

IV-11 Polynomial High-Pass Filtering (POLYHP)

POLYHP models clutter as a slowly varying low-order polynomial along slow time and removes the estimated polynomial component.

V Deep Learning-Based Clutter Suppression

In addition to signal processing-based clutter suppression methods, we introduce two supervised DL methods that operate directly on the slow-time delay correlation matrix 𝐂∈ℂK×D\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times D} obtained from matched filtering. The objective is to learn a nonlinear mapping that suppresses clutter while preserving target responses required for accurate bistatic range-Doppler estimation. Training data are generated from the multistatic ISAC signal and clutter model described previously. Each training realization contains random receiver geometries, target positions, target velocities, clutter densities, clutter RCSs, clutter Doppler spreads, and noise realizations. The training input is the clutter-contaminated matched-filter matrix

𝐂raw=𝐂target+𝐂clutter+𝐍,\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{target}}+\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{clutter}}+\mathbf{N}, (15)

where 𝐂target\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{target}} and 𝐂clutter\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{clutter}} denote the target-only and clutter-only correlation matrices, respectively, and 𝐍\mathbf{N} denotes the additive noise. The desired output is 𝐂target\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{target}}.

Next, we present two DL-based clutter suppression (DLCS) methods that estimate 𝐂target\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{target}} from 𝐂raw\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}. The estimated target-only correlation matrix is subsequently used in (8) in place of 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m} for range-Doppler estimation.

V-A Residual U-Net-based DLCS

The first DL method, DLCS-1, employs a supervised residual U-Net architecture that directly estimates the target-only matched-filter response from clutter-corrupted observations.

V-A1 Input Representation

The input is given by

𝐗=[𝐂raw(I),𝐂raw(Q)],\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(\mathrm{I})},\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(\mathrm{Q})}], (16)

where 𝐂raw(I)\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(\mathrm{I})} and 𝐂raw(Q)\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(\mathrm{Q})} are the in-phase and quadrature components of the complex-valued correlation matrix, respectively, and are normalized using the root-mean-square (RMS) magnitude of the input tensor before being passed to the network.

V-A2 Network Architecture

The network follows an encoder-decoder U-Net structure with skip connections. The encoder consists of repeated convolutional blocks that progressively extract hierarchical clutter and target features while reducing spatial resolution through max-pooling operations. Each convolutional block contains 3×33\times 3 convolutional layers, batch normalization, and rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations.

The feature tensor 𝐅(ℓ)\mathbf{F}^{(\ell)} at layer ℓ\ell is encoded as

𝐅(ℓ+1)=ReLU⁡(BN⁡(Conv⁡(𝐅(ℓ)))),\mathbf{F}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{ReLU}\left(\mathrm{BN}\left(\mathrm{Conv}(\mathbf{F}^{(\ell)})\right)\right), (17)

where Conv⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Conv}(\cdot) denotes convolution and BN⁡(⋅)\mathrm{BN}(\cdot) denotes batch normalization. The decoder progressively reconstructs a target-enhanced residual map using bilinear upsampling and skip-connected encoder features. Skip connections preserve fine spatial structures corresponding to localized target peaks in the range-Doppler domain. The final output layer is a 1×11\times 1 convolution that produces a two-channel estimate

𝐘^=[𝐂^target(I),𝐂^target(Q)],\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=[\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}^{(\mathrm{I})},\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}^{(\mathrm{Q})}], (18)

where 𝐂^target(I)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}^{(\mathrm{I})} and 𝐂^target(Q)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}^{(\mathrm{Q})} denote the predicted in-phase and quadrature components of the target-only correlation matrix.

V-A3 Training Objective

The network is trained using a residual reconstruction loss composed of mean-squared error and sparsity regularization:

ℒDLCS=‖𝐂^target−𝐂target‖22+λ1​‖𝐂^target‖1,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DLCS}}=\left\|\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}-\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{target}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{1}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}\right\|_{1}, (19)

where λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 controls sparsity regularization. The ℓ2\ell_{2} term encourages accurate target reconstruction. The ℓ1\ell_{1} term promotes sparse target responses and suppresses residual clutter artifacts.

V-A4 Optimization

The network parameters are optimized using the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate ηDLCS=10−3\eta_{\mathrm{DLCS}}=10^{-3} and a weight-decay regularization coefficient λwd=10−5\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}=10^{-5}. Mini-batch training is used with random clutter and target realizations. Gradient clipping is applied to stabilize optimization:

‖∇θℒ‖2≤γmax,\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}\|_{2}\leq\gamma_{\max}, (20)

where θ\theta denotes the trainable network parameters and the clipping threshold γmax\gamma_{\max} is 55. After training, the output 𝐂^target\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}} is processed in the CAF and range-Doppler estimation stages.

V-B Attention-Gated Anisotropic DLCS

The second DL method, DLCS-2, extends the residual U-Net architecture through anisotropic convolutional processing and attention-gated skip connections designed specifically for clutter-dominated range-Doppler maps.

V-B1 Multi-Channel Input Representation

Instead of using only real and imaginary channels, the network exploits four complementary input representations:

𝐗=[𝐂raw(I),𝐂raw(Q),|𝐂raw|,log⁡(1+|𝐂raw|)].\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(\mathrm{I})},\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(\mathrm{Q})},|\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}|,\log(1+|\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}|)]. (21)

The magnitude channel explicitly captures target energy distributions, while the logarithmic channel compresses dynamic range and improves representation of weak target responses in strong clutter environments.

V-B2 Anisotropic Convolutional Encoder

The encoder uses anisotropic convolutional blocks that separately model slow-time and delay-domain structures. Each anisotropic block contains standard 3×33\times 3 convolutions, elongated (5×1)(5\times 1) convolutions, elongated (1×5)(1\times 5) convolutions, batch normalization, and ReLU nonlinearities. The (5×1)(5\times 1) kernels learn slow-time Doppler structures and clutter trajectories, whereas the (1×5)(1\times 5) kernels learn range-domain correlations and delay-spread clutter structures. Let 𝐅\mathbf{F} denote an intermediate feature map. An anisotropic block computes 𝐅st=Conv5×1​(𝐅)\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{st}}=\mathrm{Conv}_{5\times 1}(\mathbf{F}) and 𝐅rg=Conv1×5​(𝐅)\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{rg}}=\mathrm{Conv}_{1\times 5}(\mathbf{F}), followed by nonlinear feature fusion. This directional processing better distinguishes between target signatures and clutter structures that exhibit different geometric behavior across delay and slow-time dimensions.

V-B3 Attention-Gated Skip Connections

The decoder incorporates attention-gated skip connections to suppress clutter-dominated encoder activations before feature fusion. Let 𝐒\mathbf{S} denote the encoder skip feature map and 𝐆\mathbf{G} denote the decoder gating feature map. The attention mask is computed as 𝐀=σ⁡(ψ⁡(ϕ⁡(𝐒)+θ⁡(𝐆)))\mathbf{A}=\sigma\left(\psi\left(\phi(\mathbf{S})+\theta(\mathbf{G})\right)\right), where ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot), θ⁡(⋅)\theta(\cdot), and ψ⁡(⋅)\psi(\cdot) are learned convolutional transformations and σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid activation function. The refined skip feature becomes 𝐒att=𝐀⊙𝐒\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{att}}=\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{S}, where ⊙\odot denotes elementwise multiplication. This mechanism suppresses clutter-dominated feature activations while preserving target-dominant spatial structures by emphasizing features consistent with the decoder’s target-relevant context.

V-B4 Decoder Structure

The decoder reconstructs the target-enhanced residual map through bilinear upsampling and feature concatenation with the attention-refined skip features. Each decoder stage employs anisotropic convolutional blocks similar to those used in the encoder. Anisotropic convolutions employ direction-dependent convolution kernels with unequal spatial support across dimensions. Kernels of size 5×15\times 1 and 1×51\times 5 are used to separately model slow-time Doppler structures and delay-domain correlations, respectively. The final output layer generates a two-channel estimate of the target residual:

𝐘^=[𝐂^target(I),𝐂^target(Q)].\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=[\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}^{(\mathrm{I})},\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}^{(\mathrm{Q})}]. (22)

V-B5 Loss Function

The network is trained using a combination of reconstruction and sparsity losses:

ℒAttn\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Attn}} =‖𝐂^target−𝐂target‖22+λs​‖𝐂^target‖1\displaystyle=\left\|\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}-\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{target}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{s}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}\right\|_{1}
+λTV​TV​(𝐂^target),\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{\mathrm{TV}}\mathrm{TV}(\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathrm{target}}), (23)

where λs\lambda_{s} controls sparsity regularization and λTV\lambda_{\mathrm{TV}} controls total-variation regularization. The total-variation term promotes spatial smoothness while preserving localized target peaks.

V-B6 Optimization and Training

Training is performed using the AdamW optimizer with mini-batch gradient descent. Gradient clipping and weight decay are applied to improve optimization stability and generalization performance. After training, the network output is directly processed using CAF-based range-Doppler estimation and bistatic localization.

VI Performance Evaluation

For the numerical results, we assume a transmit power of 40 dBm, transmit and receive antenna gains of 10 dBi, a target RCS of 4 m2\mathrm{m}^{2}, and a noise variance of 10−310^{-3}. All DL models were trained using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. The DLCS-1 and DLCS-2 architectures contain 1,885,186 and 12,398,789 trainable parameters, respectively. Let NtrainN_{\mathrm{train}} and NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} denote the numbers of training and test samples, respectively, and let NepochN_{\mathrm{epoch}} denote the number of training epochs. For each sample, the transmitter and receiver geometry, target position and velocity, clutter scatterer locations, and additive noise realizations are randomly generated. Clutter effects are controlled by the values of NcN_{c}, αc\alpha_{c}, and σf,c\sigma_{f,c}. The training and test data are generated independently, with clutter density, strength, and Doppler spread randomized during training.

We first consider a moderate training setting of Ntrain=500N_{\mathrm{train}}\!=\!500 and Nepoch=200N_{\mathrm{epoch}}\!=\!200 under a strong clutter environment with Nc=40N_{c}\!=\!40, αc=1\alpha_{c}\!=\!1, and σf,c=30\sigma_{f,c}\!=\!30 Hz. For a randomly selected test sample (Ntest=1N_{\mathrm{test}}\!=\!1), Tables I and II compare DLCS-1 with NCS and RMHP. NCS produces severe bistatic-range and radial-velocity estimation errors, leading to large localization and velocity estimation errors, as shown in Figs. 2 and 3. RMHP, the strongest conventional baseline, improves the estimates by suppressing slowly varying clutter, but fails to accurately recover the target response for the other receivers, causing large localization and velocity-estimation errors. DLCS-1 accurately estimates bistatic range and radial velocity for all receivers, achieving a position error of 4.462 m and speed and angle estimation errors of only 0.445 m/s and 0.045∘0.045^{\circ}, respectively.

The range-Doppler maps in Fig. 4 further illustrate these performance differences. For NCS and RMHP, clutter obscures the target response, causing large estimation errors. In contrast, DLCS-1 produces cleaner range-Doppler maps with localized target peaks closely aligned with the true target locations. As a result, DLCS-1 achieves highly accurate velocity estimation (Fig. 2) and target localization (Fig. 3).

Next, we increase the number of test samples to Ntest=2000N_{\mathrm{test}}=2000 and statistically compare DLCS-1 with conventional clutter-suppression baselines under different clutter settings specified by NcN_{c}, αc\alpha_{c}, and σf,c\sigma_{f,c}. For each clutter case, the success rate is defined as the percentage of trials with position error below T=10T=10 m, and ηsucc\eta_{\text{succ}} is computed as the normalized success rate relative to the reference method CUR of Sec. IV-2.

As shown in Table III, DLCS-1 consistently achieves a higher normalized success rate ηsucc\eta_{\text{succ}} than all non-reference clutter-suppression methods across all clutter environments. Conventional methods degrade significantly under dense and dynamic clutter. RMHP is the strongest conventional baseline, yet remains substantially outperformed by DLCS-1.

Table IV compares ηsucc\eta_{\text{succ}} of DLCS-1 and DLCS-2 for different clutter and training configurations. As NtrainN_{\mathrm{train}} and NepochN_{\mathrm{epoch}} increase to 5000 and 500, respectively, DLCS-2 approaches the performance of the reference method while consistently outperforming DLCS-1 across all clutter settings.

Fig. 5 shows ηsucc\eta_{\text{succ}} as a function of position error threshold TT. Across all TT and clutter settings, the DLCS methods, trained with Ntrain=5000N_{\mathrm{train}}=5000 and Nepoch=500N_{\mathrm{epoch}}=500, consistently outperform NCS and RMHP. DLCS-2 achieves the best performance, followed closely by DLCS-1, demonstrating the effectiveness of DL-based clutter suppression in multistatic ISAC.

VII Conclusion

In this paper, we studied clutter suppression in multistatic ISAC using 5G NR PRS for bistatic range-Doppler estimation, target localization, and velocity estimation in dense and dynamic clutter environments. We showed that clutter can severely degrade sensing accuracy of multistatic ISAC and that conventional signal processing methods for clutter suppression provide only limited gains under challenging clutter conditions. To improve robustness of multistatic ISAC against clutter, we introduced DL-based clutter suppression methods to directly enhance target responses from clutter-corrupted observations. These methods substantially improve clutter suppression and reduce sensing errors relative to conventional approaches across diverse clutter conditions in multistatic ISAC.
